name: St Peter's Church, Wootton Wawen
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church in Wootton Wawen, on the train's {side}, said to be the oldest church in Warwickshire. The lower stages of its central tower are Anglo-Saxon, the most marked Saxon work in the county, from a church built by a landowner called Wagen, who gave the village its name.

name: Edstone Aqueduct
text: Your train passes under Edstone Aqueduct, which carries the Stratford-upon-Avon Canal over the line, a road, a stream and a field. Built between 1812 and 1816 from 35 cast iron sections bolted together on 13 brick piers, it is the longest cast iron aqueduct in England, with its towpath set level with the bottom of the trough.

name: Mary Arden's Farm
text: Your train passes near Mary Arden's Farm, on the train's {side}, the home of William Shakespeare's mother, now kept as a working Tudor farm by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. Both its farmhouses are listed Grade I: in 2000 it was found that the one long shown as Mary Arden's had in fact belonged to a neighbour, Adam Palmer.

name: Wilmcote
text: Your train passes near the village of Wilmcote, on the train's {side}, once known for its limestone quarries. The Stratford-upon-Avon Canal, opened in 1816, was routed through the village because of them, and the blue-grey Wilmcote stone was used in building Shakespeare's Birthplace.

name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
text: Your train passes near Shakespeare's Birthplace on Henley Street, on the train's {side}, the half-timbered house where William Shakespeare is believed to have been born in 1564. His father, John, a glove maker and wool dealer, worked from part of the house; it is now a museum run by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

name: Bearley station
text: Bearley station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1860 on the line from Hatton to Stratford-upon-Avon and was once a junction: a branch to Alcester met the line here from 1876 until it closed in 1951. Today it is an unstaffed halt with no trains on Sundays.

name: Pinley Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Pinley Priory, on the train's {side}, a Cistercian nunnery founded in the early 12th century and closed in 1536. Little of it survives, but a farmhouse of the mid-15th century there takes in part of a wall thought to belong to an earlier monastic building, and a nearby cottage was probably the nuns' guest house.

name: Shrewley Tunnel
text: Your train passes near Shrewley Tunnel, on the train's {side}, which takes the Grand Union Canal under the village of Shrewley. Opened in 1799, it has no towpath, so the horses that pulled the boats went through a separate tunnel of their own, climbing a ramp at the northern end and crossing the road above.

name: Kingswood
text: Your train passes near Kingswood, on the train's {side}, where the Grand Union and Stratford-upon-Avon canals meet at Kingswood Junction. The station that serves it was first called Kingswood too, but it was renamed Lapworth to avoid confusion with the station of the same name in Surrey.

name: Dorridge
text: Your train passes near Dorridge, on the train's {side}, a village that barely existed until the Great Western Railway built this line in 1852, to Brunel's seven-foot gauge. The Muntz family gave the land on condition that a station was built, and in the 1960s and 1970s the Austin Motor Company sent up to 600 cars a day for export from its goods yard.

name: St Alphege Church, Solihull
text: Your train passes near St Alphege Church in Solihull, on the train's {side}, a cross-shaped medieval church begun in the 13th century and listed Grade I. Its first spire collapsed in 1757; the one that replaced it is about 57 metres tall.

name: Olton Reservoir
text: Your train passes near Olton Reservoir, or Olton Mere, on the train's {side}, made from marshland in 1799 to feed water to the canal that is now the Grand Union. It was meant to hold enough water to fill 150 locks, but only did once it was enlarged in 1834; today it is home to a sailing club.

name: St Mary the Virgin, Acocks Green
text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary the Virgin in Acocks Green, on the train's {side}, begun in 1864 when the growing village wanted a parish church of its own. The tower, spire and transepts it was designed with were never built, and damage from a bomb in December 1940 can still be seen inside.

name: Hay Hall
text: Your train passes near Hay Hall, on the train's {side}, a hall of the 15th century that now stands among factories on a business park. A moated house was first built here in about 1275; the tube company that bought the estate in 1917 built its works around the hall but saved it from demolition.

name: Hatton Locks
text: Your train passes near Hatton Locks, on the train's {side}, a flight of 21 locks that lifts the Grand Union Canal up the hill towards Birmingham. Built for single narrowboats in 1799, they were rebuilt wide enough for two side by side in the 1930s, and the new locks were opened by Prince George, Duke of Kent, in October 1934.

name: Collegiate Church of St Mary, Warwick
text: Your train passes near the Collegiate Church of St Mary in Warwick, on the train's {side}, founded in 1123. Its nave and tower were destroyed in the Great Fire of Warwick in 1693 and rebuilt, but the Norman crypt survives, and the Beauchamp Chapel holds the tombs of Earls of Warwick and of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester.

name: St John's House, Warwick
text: Your train passes near St John's House in Warwick, on the train's {side}, a house of about 1666 listed Grade I. It stands on the site of the Hospital of St John the Baptist, founded in the 12th century to help the poor and the sick and to give food and a bed to travellers such as pilgrims.

name: St Mary's Abbey, Kenilworth
text: Your train passes near the remains of St Mary's Abbey in Kenilworth, on the train's {side}, founded as a priory in 1119 by Geoffrey de Clinton, who also built Kenilworth Castle. Made an abbey in 1447, it was surrendered to Henry VIII in 1538; its ruins lie beside St Nicholas' Church and in Abbey Fields, and its gatehouse and barn survive.

name: Ford's Hospital
text: Your train passes near Ford's Hospital in Coventry, on the train's {side}, a half-timbered almshouse founded by the merchant William Ford in 1509 for six elderly people. Hit by bombs in 1940, it was restored with its original timbers in the early 1950s, and Shakespeare scholars have studied its doorways to help reconstruct the Globe Theatre.

name: Stoney Road Allotments
text: Your train passes near Stoney Road Allotments, on the train's {side}, laid out soon after 1853 as pleasure gardens for the people of Coventry. The 123 plots were listed Grade II* in 2001 because they keep features of the old gardens, including summer houses and glasshouses of the period.

name: Canley
text: Your train passes near Canley, on the train's {side}, farmland until 1916, when the Standard Motor Company built its main factory here, first making fighter aircraft for the First World War. Standard and then Triumph cars were made at Canley until car production stopped in August 1980.

name: Nailcote Hall
text: Your train passes near Nailcote Hall, on the train's {side}, a house built in 1640, just before the Civil War, and damaged by Cromwell's troops during it. The Lant family lived there for some 300 years; it is now a country house hotel.

name: Hampton in Arden packhorse bridge
text: Your train passes near the packhorse bridge over the River Blythe, on the train's {side}, built in the 15th century for traders leading horses laden with goods to market. It is the only bridge of its kind in the West Midlands, and has been called the longest surviving packhorse bridge in England.

name: National Exhibition Centre
text: Your train passes near the National Exhibition Centre, on the train's {side}, opened by Queen Elizabeth II on February 2nd 1976 after Leicestershire turned down plans to build it beside the M1. It has grown to 18 connected halls, and has been home to the Motor Show and the dog show Crufts.

name: Air-Rail Link
text: Your train passes near the Air-Rail Link, on the train's {side}, a cable-hauled shuttle between the station and Birmingham Airport. It runs mostly on the guideway of the Birmingham Maglev, which opened in 1984 as the first commercial maglev in the world and closed in 1995 when spare parts ran out.

name: Our Lady Help of Christians, Tile Cross
text: Your train passes near the church of Our Lady Help of Christians in Tile Cross, on the train's {side}, built in 1966 and 1967 to a design by Richard Gilbert Scott, son of Giles Gilbert Scott. Its altar stands forward among the congregation, and above it part of the roof is made of curved, saw-toothed concrete trusses clad in copper outside.

name: Stechford Baptist Church
text: Your train passes near Stechford Baptist Church, on the train's {side}, whose building went up in 1926 as a Canadian timber frame expected to last about ten years until a brick church replaced it. The brick church was never built, and the church has become known for its work against racism since the 1960s.

name: Adderley Park
text: Your train passes near Adderley Park, on the train's {side}, opened to the public on August 30th 1856 on land given by the MP Charles Adderley. The area was later home to Wolseley Motors, from 1901; its works made vans until early 1972.

name: Coventry Building Society Arena
text: Your train passes near the Coventry Building Society Arena, on the train's {side}, home of Coventry City, built on the site of the Foleshill gasworks. Once called the Ricoh Arena, its 32,609-seat stadium was used for football at the 2012 Olympics and for rugby sevens at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.

name: The Charterhouse, Coventry
text: Your train passes near the Charterhouse in Coventry, on the train's {side}, a Carthusian priory whose foundation stone was laid by Richard II and Anne of Bohemia on September 6th 1385. Its wall painting of the Crucifixion, from about 1417, is the only medieval wall painting to survive in a Carthusian monastery in England.

name: St Botolph's Church, Newbold-on-Avon
text: Your train passes near St Botolph's Church in Newbold-on-Avon, on the train's {side}, a pink sandstone church of the 15th century that looks over the River Avon. Inside are many monuments to the Boughton family of nearby Lawford Hall, the earliest from 1454.

name: Nuneaton Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Nuneaton Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of nuns founded in about 1155 that gave the town its name: Eaton became Nuneaton. It held 93 nuns in 1234 and was closed by Henry VIII in 1539; the parish church of St Mary the Virgin was later built on its old foundations.

name: Water Orton Bridge
text: Your train passes near the old bridge over the River Tame at Water Orton, on the train's {side}, a sandstone bridge built in 1520 by Bishop John Vesey of Sutton Coldfield. It replaced an earlier bridge that was already in a poor state in the 1460s, and is a scheduled monument.

name: Kingsbury Hall
text: Your train passes near Kingsbury Hall, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house whose curtain wall can still be seen, now partly lived in as a farmhouse. In 1474 Alice Bracebridge of the hall married John Arden, of the family of Shakespeare's mother, after a family dispute so bitter that Edward IV appointed two knights to settle it.

name: Whitacre Pumping Station
text: Your train passes near Whitacre Pumping Station, on the train's {side}, a Victorian waterworks built to pump six million gallons of water a day to Birmingham. It started in 1883, but once the Elan Valley reservoirs in Wales began to supply Birmingham it was put on standby, and from 1908 it supplied Coventry instead.

name: Bolehall Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Bolehall Viaduct, known locally as the 19 Arches, over the River Anker on the edge of Tamworth. Designed by George Stephenson for the Birmingham and Derby Junction Railway, it carried its first train on July 6th 1839 and is still in use.

name: Tamworth Castle
text: Your train passes near Tamworth Castle, on the train's {side}, in a town that was the main seat of the Mercian kings in the 8th and 9th centuries. The Normans built a motte and bailey partly on the site of the Saxon fort, and the Marmion family replaced it with the sandstone castle that stands today.

name: St Nicholas' Church, Mavesyn Ridware
text: Your train passes near the church of St Nicholas in Mavesyn Ridware, on the train's {side}, said to have been founded in 1140 by Hugo de Mavesyn. In 1782 all but its medieval tower and north aisle were pulled down and rebuilt in red brick, and the old aisle became a family chapel; the church is listed Grade I.

name: Lichfield Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Lichfield Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built of red sandstone, mostly between the early 13th century and about 1320. Its three spires are known as the Ladies of the Vale; the central one, pulled down during the Civil War and later rebuilt, is 77 metres tall.

name: Hospital of St John Baptist without the Barrs
text: Your train passes near the Hospital of St John Baptist without the Barrs, on the train's {side}, founded in 1135 to give a bed to pilgrims and travellers who reached Lichfield after the city gates had shut for the night. Its row of eight Tudor chimneys dates from its time as an almshouse for elderly men.
